item.title: This French City Was Rarely Linked With Unrest. Then Arsonists Attacked.
item.description:
Gathered in the heart of Limoges, a small city in central France, more than a hundred people gazed in shock on Sunday afternoon at what remained of their city hall.

Some stood in silence. Others took pictures of the building’s skeletal frame, still smoking from a fire that had largely destroyed it the night before.

Apart from the building’s gray stone walls, erected in the late 19th century, and a few broken windows, not much remained. Not the roof, not the clock on the facade, not even the metal bell tower that once loomed over the building.

“All we have left are pictures,” said Gilles Peignelin, 64, who was staring at the ruin alongside his wife, Sylvie, 61. They married in the building 35 years ago, they said, recalling its grand staircase and painting collection. Now, that staircase seemed to have collapsed, Mr. Peignelin noted, pointing through a shattered window.

“I’m outraged — it’s shameful, deplorable,” Ms. Peignelin added.

The damage at Limoges was among the most serious and surprising stemming from the nationwide unrest that swept across France yesterday, as huge anti-government marches gave way to rioting.

Some 2,000 people were arrested nationwide as rioters attacked government buildings and roughly 1,500 shops.

Limoges, a quiet city renowned for its porcelain and far from the unrest of Paris, is the only place that saw its city hall burn down, though a tourist office was also set on fire in Lyon.

The rallies in the city, which has roughly 130,000 residents, began relatively calmly, the authorities said. Several thousands demonstrators marched through the streets in the late morning to protest rising living costs and express solidarity with high school students calling for better school conditions.

The authorities said that rioters headed toward the city center at 5 p.m. with the “sole objective to burn, break and loot.” By 6 p.m., rioters forced their way into the city hall and set it on fire while staff and visitors were still inside, the authorities said. Despite firefighters’ swift response, the building was largely destroyed — with its burning bell tower toppling over several hours later.

“Today, the entire facade and the historic front section have been almost 100 percent destroyed,” Maurice Barate, the top official for the region, announced on national television. Mr. Barate said that firefighters had been disadvantaged by the wind, and that the city hall’s wooden roof had “collapsed onto the rest of the building.”

Listed as a historical monument, Limoges’s city hall was built by a Parisian architect, Charles-Alfred Leclerc, in the 1880s. A jewel of late-19th-century French architecture, the building featured a metal bell tower, ornate details on its facade and mosaic portraits of local figures. At the start of World War II, the monument hosted exiled Belgian lawmakers after Belgium surrendered to Nazi Germany.

Many saw the burning of the hall as a direct assault on the French state.

To attack the city hall is “to attack the Republic,” said Guillaume Guérin, the Limoges mayor, on social media on Sunday morning. Mr. Guérin, of the main conservative party, the Republicans, also accused the perpetrators of being affiliated with or manipulated by the far left and promised to hold them accountable.

The local prosecutor’s office has announced that 17 people were arrested in the city this weekend, including seven minors, though it did not clarify if they were accused of involvement in the arson.

Lino Cardona, an art student who joined the peaceful protests earlier in the day, said the atmosphere at the demonstrations turned sour as soon as the city hall attack began.

“That’s when the joyful, inclusive atmosphere disappeared,” said Ms. Cardona, 26, who lamented how the violence would now overshadow the goals of the peaceful protesters.

The attack was a powerful symbol of “the fragility of our institutions,” she added. “We now need to ask ourselves: How do we move forward?”

The Peignelins said they were shocked at how such violence could reach a city usually untouched by unrest — and they were angry at the government’s failure to prevent it.

“We didn’t expect this in Limoges, but today we realize that even a small town in France can be a hotbed of chaos,” Mr. Peignelin said.

Ms. Peignelin added: “I’m sickened by a government that does nothing. We know full well that the people who did this won’t be brought to justice.”

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu and other government leaders have pledged consequences for perpetrators across France, including by making them pay for the damage. In a message to Mr. Guérin, the mayor, that was reviewed by The New York Times, Mr. Lecornu said the state would help cover costs from the blaze and pledged to visit the city this week.

Mr. Guérin complained that the national government had done too little to prevent the fire, saying that local law enforcement “had simply run out of ammunition” by 3:30 p.m. on Saturday.

“This country is in bad shape,” Mr. Guérin said, adding, “If there isn’t a change in policy, if there isn’t a shift in direction, things are going to end very, very badly.”

item.title: U.S. Officials Condemn West Bank Attacks as Netanyahu Casts Doubt on Them
item.description:
American and European officials have condemned a spate of violence in the West Bank, as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel sought to cast doubt on the attacks.

Israeli extremist attacks against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank have escalated in recent weeks amid the annual olive harvest. On Friday, masked assailants were filmed beating Heidi Levine, an American photographer for the Washington Post covering the harvest outside of Ramallah.

Marco Rubio, the U.S. secretary of state, said on Saturday that the Trump administration was “very disturbed” by the footage and was seeking more information about the attacks. He said Washington had “asked the Israelis and continue to ask them to crack down on that stuff.”

Mike Huckabee, the U.S. ambassador to Israel, said on Saturday night on social media that the attack on Ms. Levine was “a despicable act of terror,” and called on the authorities to prosecute those responsible to the fullest extent of the law.

Earlier on Saturday, masked men had attacked Palestinians and a European diplomatic convoy in the Christian town of Taybeh, where they had been participating in the olive harvest. Bernard Baudoux, a visiting French mayor, was also attacked, according to the French foreign ministry.

The European Union denounced the violence and, in a statement on Sunday, the French foreign ministry called on Israel to take measures to stop “these acts of terror.”

In public statements over the weekend, Mr. Netanyahu allowed that there was a “scourge of violence” but said what happened in the attacks was still unclear, despite video footage of them. His office also said they may be part of “a coordinated campaign to smear Israel.”

The attacks come at a sensitive moment for Israel’s government. The country will hold elections later this month that are widely seen as a referendum on Mr. Netanyahu’s leadership.

His opponents say they will rein in Israeli settler attacks on Palestinians. Gadi Eisenkot, Mr. Netanyahu’s leading opponent in next week’s vote, said the current government was allowing “Jewish terrorism” to rage in the West Bank.

Since late September, when the harvest began, more than 80 violent episodes involving Israeli soldiers and settlers have been reported, according to Yesh Din, an Israeli human rights group. The assaults are the latest in a surge of violence over the past few years that has driven out entire Palestinian communities in the West Bank.

Ms. Levine was covering the olive harvest when her assailants knocked her down and beat her with sticks, breaking her rib, lacerating her legs and hip, and giving her a serious cut on her left hand, her family said.

As criticism mounted this weekend, Mr. Netanyahu sought to downplay the events, saying more needed to be learned. In a television interview that aired on Saturday night, the prime minister said he did not support “vigilantism,” but cast doubt on whether the attack on Ms. Levine took place as described.

“This is being looked into — many times now, it’s been said that something happened, but it turned out that it didn’t,” Mr. Netanyahu told the i24 news broadcaster.

When the interviewer pressed him about videos that showed Ms. Levine on the ground, surrounded by her masked assailants, Mr. Netanyahu demurred. “I don’t know, we’re checking that,” he said, adding that he was not willing to accept such violence.

In an interview with Israel’s Channel 12, Ms. Levine called Mr. Netanyahu’s account of the attack “such a lie and the biggest insult.”

The Israeli prime minister currently faces a tight election battle on Oct. 27, with opinion polls suggesting that his allies and opponents are nearly tied. That leaves the prime minister fighting to shore up support among his right-wing base.

Many of Mr. Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition partners, including the national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, have not publicly denounced the attacks over the weekend. A spokesman for Mr. Ben-Gvir did not immediately comment.

President Trump encouraged Israelis to vote for Mr. Netanyahu on Sunday in a post on social media, saying that “the wrong Leader” would be “anyone other than Bibi,” referring to Mr. Netanyahu by his nickname.

Isaac Herzog, the Israeli president, said on Saturday night that he had spoken with Ms. Levine to condemn the assault, which he said had “weighed heavily on my conscience.” Mr. Herzog holds a largely ceremonial role as Israel’s official head of state without any political authority.

“The despicable behavior of the perpetrators of this attack does not represent the citizens or the values of the State of Israel,” Mr. Herzog said in a statement.

More than 100 retired Israeli diplomats, including former ambassadors, signed an open letter on Saturday in which they condemned the attacks as a “moral stain that will not easily be erased.” They also argued that it was causing “unacceptable damage to Israel’s foreign relations.”

item.title: Fire at Canadian Army Base Killed 4 and Injured Dozens
item.description:
Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada said on Sunday that four members of the country’s military had been killed in a “violent, fast-moving” fire at an army base southeast of Edmonton, and dozens of others were seriously injured.

The fire erupted just after 4 p.m. local time on Saturday at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, one of the country’s busiest army bases.

“What followed was one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime,” Mr. Carney told reporters in Ottawa on Sunday afternoon.

He did not say how many people were hospitalized because of the fire, nor what had caused the blaze.

Local authorities had said on Saturday that the flames appeared to be fanned by strong winds and “crossed the base fence” before crews were able to tame the spread around 11 p.m., about seven hours after the first calls about it came in.

Mr. Carney said he has asked senior officials to provide a detailed account later on Sunday of how the incident unfolded, and did not take any questions following his remarks.

“Canadians come together in crisis,” Mr. Carney said. “That is the best of our country.”

The Canadian flag will be lowered to half-staff on federal buildings to honor the victims, he said, and thanked medics and ambulance crews for pouring in to help from across Alberta.

C.F.B. Wainwright hosts at least two large-scale training exercises for live-fire training every October, according to the Canadian Army.

The base employs around 300 civilian workers and is in a rural area just south of the town of Wainwright, which has a population of about 6,000.

The fire comes just before a vote on Monday in which the oil-rich Western province will ask its citizens whether they want to remain part of Canada or hold a second, binding referendum on seceding. An early-voting station in Wainwright stayed open longer than scheduled on Saturday because of the fire, according to Elections Alberta.

The Department of National Defense said on Sunday that it was in the process of notifying the families of those who were injured or killed.

Cathy Keane, who is running for mayor in Oro-Medonte, a town in southern Ontario, said that her son was among those injured in the fire. Ms. Keane, in a statement posted to her social media, said she would suspend her campaigning activities to travel west to Alberta. “As a mother, right now I need to be with my son and family,” Ms. Keane said in the statement.

Condolences from political and military figures flooded in on Sunday. Pete Hoekstra, the U.S. ambassador to Canada, said in a statement that his “heart is heavy for the Canadian Armed Forces community.”

Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, the chair of the NATO Military Committee, thanked emergency medical workers for responding to the tragedy.

“Wainwright is where Canadian soldiers, and so many Allies with them, train for the hardest tasks of our profession,” he said in a post on X.

item.title: Search Continues for 11 Passengers From Capsized Boat Off Mexico Coast
item.description:
The Coast Guard is continuing a search for 11 people after their boat capsized early Friday, 140 miles from Ensenada, Mexico, on the Pacific Coast.

Emergency crews were able to rescue 16 people, as divers from the U.S. Coast Guard rappelled from helicopters to reach the passengers who were floating amid debris. The boat was no longer in sight when the Coast Guard arrived.

Those rescued were taken to a base in San Diego and then to area hospitals. Three survivors suffered injuries consistent with shark bites, Petty Officer Charlie Valor, of the Coast Guard, said in an interview on Sunday.

Two of the 16 survivors are Mexican nationals, the Coast Guard said. The Mexican Navy was assisting in the search, the authorities said.

The boat’s point of departure and destination remain unclear, as do the circumstances that caused it to capsize. It was unknown if the vessel was being operated for commercial, recreational or other purposes.

The Coast Guard received a distress call around 1 a.m. on Friday after reports of a boat “taking on water.”

A mix of aircraft and ships responded to the area, 69 miles west of San Clemente Island.

Helicopter crews saw the remnants of a capsized boat when they arrived around an hour after the distress call. Officials said they planned to continue to search for the 11 missing — until there is reason to believe they may not be alive.

“There is a chance that there could still be survivors in the water,” Petty Officer Valor said.

On Sunday, the Coast Guard confirmed that Homeland Security Investigations would lead an inquiry into the accident, instead of the Coast Guard Investigative Service unit.

The Pacific Ocean off the coast of Baja California and Southern California has become a popular route for migrant smugglers. In 2023, eight people died when their boat capsized in what the authorities described as a human smuggling operation gone awry. Two similar episodes last year, one in May and one in November, left a total of at least seven people dead.

In all three of those episodes, the passengers were riding in panga boats, open boats that can carry people or drugs.

Two Mexican citizens pleaded guilty earlier this year in connection with the four deaths in the May 2025 accident, in which prosecutors said the passengers paid smugglers about $13,500 per person.

Remy Tumin and Simon Romero contributed reporting.

item.title: To Find Criminals and Child Exploitation in Gold Mines, We Just Had to Look
item.description:
In the past year, I’ve seen toddlers working in gold mines. I’ve met miners who pay a drug cartel for the right to dig, and watched a boy drink from an underground mine’s wastewater pipe. I met workers in Colombia whose hands tremble from mercury poisoning.

One thing they have in common is that they supply gold to the supposedly tightly controlled marketplace of Wall Street financiers, central banks and government mints.

As my colleagues and I unraveled how that was possible, we kept coming back to one key point: The people who are supposed to keep dirty gold out of the legitimate marketplace rarely actually visit the mines.

That’s the gaping hole at the center of the world’s mainstream gold market. The industry has layers of people tasked with certifying that supplies are free from abuse and criminality, but nobody makes them leave their desks in places like London and Geneva.

The Times this week reported that the London Bullion Market Association, the closest thing the industry has to a regulator, has repeatedly allowed gold into the market that has been mined by criminal gangs, a drug cartel and children. In one case, we found the association helped a refiner paper over apparent violations.

Human rights abuses and criminality are often obvious, if you show up and ask. Earlier this year, I visited a mine in Northern Colombia, where miners told us they pay a drug cartel for the right work there. The gold was certified as meeting the industry’s highest standards, and was sold to a supplier of the U.S. Mint.

Similarly, my colleagues revealed that President Trump hurriedly allowed gold imports from Venezuela before independent inspectors could visit the mines and before traders had finished their due diligence.

Venezuelan mines are notoriously linked to corruption and criminality; the national gold company is designated a U.S. security threat. The importer hired one of the world’s top supply-chain experts, who praised the import plan without ever visiting the mines.

A Times reporter visited and quickly found that gangs were profiting from the gold.

I visited mines in Madagascar where children panned for gold in raw sewage and workers hammered rock, with no helmets or shoes, in shafts hundreds of feet deep. Adolescents said the pull of gold is stronger than that of school.

“I’ve already tasted money,” said a 15-year-old boy named Fredo who hauls 20-liter water tanks for miners.

Four decades ago, the Bank of England regulated the gold market, effectively as an arm of the British government. But in 1987, it passed its oversight to the L.B.M.A., an industry group run by the world’s biggest banks and refiners.

For years the L.B.M.A. was mainly concerned with gold purity and weight, not rights abuses and environmental damage. Gold was so much cheaper then. So illegal gold mining, while problematic, was not nearly as profitable, widespread and catastrophic.

But over the past two decades, wealthy investors and governments fueled a price run-up that sent gold to record highs (today’s price is roughly four times what it was in 2010). A destructive illegal-mining boom followed in some of the world’s poorest places.

Miners, and criminals who profit from them, have rushed into areas that are ecologically and politically sensitive, and often dangerous.

Brazilian gangs have moved mining barges hundreds of miles upriver, into some of the Amazon’s most remote corners. Gold mines have dumped millions of tons of waste into Papua New Guinea’s rivers. Close to 200 people have died this year at mines in Uganda, the Central African Republic, Sudan and Sumatra.

In an effort to fight the worst abuses, the United States and the European Union passed laws attempting to exclude so-called “conflict minerals” from the global supply.

In response, the L.B.M.A. issued rules aimed at eliminating money laundering, corruption, organized crime and child abuse from the supply chain. Since 2012, refiners have had to conduct annual audits to show that they followed those rules.

One major requirement: Refiners who process gold from small-scale operations must inspect the mines. This is different from government inspections. Officials in corrupt governments or countries with weak human rights records have an incentive to say that their gold is mined cleanly. The industry inspections are meant to ensure it.

But loopholes and lax enforcement mean inspections don’t always happen. If gold from a high-risk mine passes through a middleman, for example, the refiner can obscure its source. That’s how drug cartel gold ended up at the U.S. Mint and the Royal Canadian Mint. The drug connections melted away in a cauldron of gold in Texas.

In Madagascar, gold from unlicensed mines sailed into the legitimate marketplace. Despite the L.B.M.A.’s written rules, the refiner said it did not need to inspect the mines itself. The gold was certified as meeting the highest levels in the industry.

item.title: How Did Life Arise?
item.description:
Photo illustration by Will Warasila for The New York Times

Where did it start? How did it grow complex? Why did it get big? Three moments in Earth’s early history when evolution suddenly, inexplicably turned up the dial.

By William J. BroadKenneth Chang and Carl Zimmer

Life on planet Earth is a riot of diversity: ants and elephants, frogs and blue whales, tulips and redwoods, even a branch of the great apes known as humans. Uniting it all is biochemistry, in particular the shared biochemistry of genetic inheritance — DNA and RNA, the universal instruction kits of life.

Tracing these biochemical threads back through time has convinced many scientists that all life descends from a so-called Last Universal Common Ancestor, or LUCA, that emerged between 4 billion and 4.5 billion years ago, after Earth itself congealed from the gas and detritus of a nascent solar system. How this LUCA rose from the primordial stew may be impossible to ever say definitively. No fossils exist to provide a window onto that moment in time, and scientists have no point of comparison: So far, Earth is the only place in the universe known to harbor life.

After that initial “how,” the questions become marginally easier for scientists to address. Here’s what’s known about three of the biggest inflection points in the evolution of life on Earth.

4 Billion Years Ago:

Scientists agree on little regarding the origins of life, including where it might have arisen — at Earth’s surface, or in its watery depths.

“It’s hard to answer these questions,” said Joanna Masel, a professor of evolutionary biology at the University of Arizona. “The evidence is sketchy. So people argue.”

On one side is the primordial soup hypothesis: Life originated from natural chemical reactions in Earth’s primal waters, which formed a broth of organic compounds.

Charles Darwin floated the idea in 1871, when he proposed that “some warm little pond” was responsible for life’s origin. A few simple chemicals and sources of energy, he suggested, such as natural heat and electricity, might have joined together to form molecules “ready to undergo still more complex changes.” These in turn would have led to the first life form: a tiny sack of chemicals able to divide and make copies of itself.

The hypothesis got its first serious test in 1953. Stanley L. Miller, then a graduate student at the University of Chicago, filled a flask with water as well as ammonia, methane and hydrogen, gases that were considered to be abundant in the early atmosphere.

Then, to mimic a lightning strike, he introduced sparks. Days later, the simple molecules had given rise to amino acids, the building blocks of proteins and virtually all planetary life.

But the amino acids never advanced in complexity, and excitement ebbed as scientists rethought the composition of the primordial air. Some years later, researchers detected amino acids in meteorites, which suggested that the building blocks of life may have rained down from the heavens, putting another potential dent in the primordial soup theory.

On the other side of the argument is the watery-depths camp. In 1977, American scientists exploring the Pacific seabed stumbled upon an alien world of volcanic vents and otherworldly ecosystems, including eerie fields of albino tube worms. They drew their energy not from sunlight, which powers surface ecosystems, starting with plants, but instead from chemicals emitted by the hot springs.

As other deep-sea ecosystems came to light, scientists proposed that all life on Earth had perhaps arisen in the depths, nurtured by a warm, steady diet of chemicals and sheltered from the killer rocks and cosmic radiation that bombarded the planet’s surface early on.

In recent years, new discoveries have bolstered both sides of the argument.

In 2009, for instance, John D. Sutherland, a chemist at the University of Manchester, in England, described a new way that the molecules of life, energized by the sun’s ultraviolet rays, could have assembled spontaneously on the surface of a primitive Earth. And in 2017, an analysis of mineral deposits in Australia suggested that surface hot springs had nurtured the land’s earliest signs of life. In 2024, an influential group of scientists voiced strong support for the finding.

Even so, the deep springs theory has also gained new support. This summer, a team led by scientists at Heinrich Heine University in Düsseldorf, Germany, proposed that the warm chemicals available in the deep sea included metals such as nickel, cobalt and palladium. These metals, the researches contend, could have served as catalysts that helped the earliest forms of life build metabolic pathways.

The growing wealth of evidence suggests that, ultimately, both camps of theorists might be right, Dr. Masel said.

“It doesn’t have to be one thing,” she said. “It’s possible that life arose at the hydrothermal vents and also a warm little pond.”

Perhaps, she added, life arose independently in disparate ecological niches that remained isolated from one another for ages.

“It looks like the early events happened really, really fast, which points to ‘first life’ not being the hardest part,” she said. “Maybe the origin of life was easier than we thought.”— William J. Broad

2 Billion Years Ago:

About two billion years ago, a new kind of cell emerged on Earth, one much bigger and more complex than the microbes that had come before. Today, these so-called eukaryotic cells inhabit our own bodies, as well as those of other animals, plants and fungi. How this new brand of cell emerged remains one of biology’s great mysteries.

“Eukaryotic” comes from a Greek term meaning “true nut,” a reference to the nucleus, the compartment in which eukaryotic cells coil their DNA. Eukaryotic cells have many other vital compartments, including thousands of mitochondria, which generate energy. The huge volume of a eukaryotic cell is supported by a scaffolding that can be quickly dismantled and reassembled; it also serves as an internal shipping network, whizzing packages of molecules from one compartment to another.

In contrast, a single-celled microbe such as Escherichia coli is far simpler. No mitochondria, no scaffolding, no nucleus; a nut-free “prokaryote.”

Eukaryotes — organisms composed of eukaryotic cells — all descend from a common ancestor, which in turn descended from ancient prokaryotes. The earliest eukaryotes were single-celled protozoans; their oldest known fossils date back 1.8 billion years. How long before that the first eukaryotes evolved, scientists can’t say.

Living organisms have offered important clues to this transition. In the past decade, scientists have discovered a lineage of microbes known as Asgards that bear many, but not all, of the hallmarks of eukaryotes. For instance, they have a cellular skeleton that helps them crawl, but have no nucleus or mitochondria.

The current thinking is that Asgards descend from the forerunners of eukaryotes. Early Asgard-like organisms acquired some eukaryote features through ordinary natural selection: Mutations altered their cells, conferring advantages they passed down to their descendants today.

But cells evolved by other means, too.

Early eukaryotes lived in close quarters with other microbes, forming ecological partnerships. That intimate contact made it possible for the early ancestors of Asgards and eukaryotes to grab genes from their partners and add them to their own genomes.

This exchange may have started about 3 billion years ago and continued for hundreds of millions of years. Recent studies suggest that the final exchange that gave rise to eukaryotes was the most spectacular. Around 2.25 billion years ago, one species of bacteria took up permanent residence inside Asgard-like cells, using their own metabolism to generate fuel for the cells they occupied. They began to be passed down from one generation of hosts to the next, evolving into our mitochondria.

The broad outlines of eukaryote origins are now coming into focus, but many pages of the story are still blank. Scientists don’t yet know how all the parts that make up the nucleus came together, for instance.

And they don’t know why the merging of microbes apparently gave rise to big, complex cells just once in the history of life. Was there some exquisitely rare set of circumstances that allowed it to happen? Or did evolution conduct other experiments in complexity that ended in extinction long ago?

One thing is clear: Once the eukaryote cell evolved, Earth was never the same. From coral reefs and giant squid to Amazonian rainforests and vast herds of wildebeest on the African savanna, eukaryotes gave rise to all the life we can see, including the one in the mirror.

— Carl Zimmer

580 Million Years Ago:

The advent of eukaryotes set up the evolutionary foundations for coral reefs and herds of wildebeest, but it took life a long time to have a growth spurt.

Indeed, the billion years that followed are often called “the boring billion.” Evolution appeared to stagnate; life stayed almost entirely microscopic. Even the tectonic plates pressed pause, leaving the continents mountainless. Then, about 720 million years ago, the world went haywire.

First, Earth froze over, sealing the planet in an icy shell that blocked sunlight from the oceans and shut off photosynthesis. Except for a 10-million-year thaw in the middle of it, Earth remained a shiny white snowball, not a blue marble, for 85 million years.

Scientists marvel that life did not die out. Instead, after that long era of darkness, it underwent a mysterious jump in size and complexity.

“That is the absolute wackiest interval of Earth history that anyone’s aware of,” said Nick Butterfield, a paleobiologist at Cambridge. “You go in the one end, and it’s this old, dreary, boring microbial world, and you come out the other end after these two massive glaciations, and all of a sudden, there’s animals on the scene, and all the microbes have changed.”

The changes were so striking that in 2006, scientists named a new geological period to encompass them: the Ediacaran. It began around 635 million years ago, with the thawing of “Snowball Earth,” and ended roughly 540 million years ago with the start of the Cambrian Era.

Guy Narbonne, a geological scientist at Queen’s University in Ontario, Canada, has studied fossils of large, soft-bodied animals that lived during the Ediacaran at a site known as Mistaken Point, at the southeastern tip of Newfoundland. The creatures include rangeomorphs, marine animals that looked like palm fronds and could reach the height of a modern-day basketball player. Others were round and the size of coins. Some, perhaps early sponges, were cone-shaped.

For Dr. Narbonne, the story is straightforward: The omnipresent glaciers crushed rocks as they moved across the landscape. When they receded, the sediment washed into the ocean, spurring algal blooms that raised oxygen levels and made possible the greater metabolism required by larger creatures.

“I can’t think of a better way of fertilizing the oceans than to have glaciers melt after the end of a glaciation,” Dr. Narbonne said.

Andrew Knoll, a paleontologist at Harvard, also thinks that oxygen fueled the evolutionary jump during the Ediacaran. But in his view, the timing of Snowball Earth was coincidental; instead, he points to the resumption of plate tectonics at the end of the boring billion, which created Himalayan-scale mountains.

As these eroded, they added phosphorus to the oceans, which seeded blooms of photosynthesizing marine microbes, Dr. Knoll said. Predators evolved and began feasting on smaller organisms, which spurred an evolutionary arms race to get bigger, in order to avoid getting eaten.

But some scientists doubt the oxygen story, including Donald Canfield, a geochemist at the University of Southern Denmark, who performed the analysis that is often cited as evidence of an oxygen increase during the early Ediacaran.

“I’ve had somewhat of a change of mind,” Dr. Canfield said. He now thinks that oxygen levels in Earth’s atmosphere then were low, but significant and steady — about 4 to 10 percent of current levels.

Dr. Butterfield, for his part, thinks that scientists have been looking at the question backward. He proposes that complex animals began to appear before Snowball Earth, not afterward, simply as the culmination of random genetic mutations. This revolution in evolution, he says, upended the food chain, altered the chemistry of the oceans, pulled carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere — and tipped the world into a frozen state. Big life caused Snowball Earth, not the other way around.

“To my eye, the single most insulting, ecologically insulting, thing that has ever been imposed on this planet,” Dr. Butterfield said, “is animals.”

— Kenneth Chang

item.title: Alberta Voting on Its Future in Canada, With Its Leader Caught in the Middle
item.description:
Surrounded by wooden plaques bearing the brands of Alberta cattlemen, a group of Alberta farmers and ranchers sat around a hotel bar discussing the vote that could set their province on a path to break away from Canada.

With Albertans about to start casting ballots, their debate captured the divisions that have cropped up in their province since secession advocates began laying the groundwork for a referendum last year.

The vote on Monday will not lead directly to secession. It instead asks voters whether they want to to remain part of Canada or if Alberta should hold a second referendum about breaking away. If it passes, it will put the province that much closer to a future some embrace and others fear.

Stuart Cannon, whose family has ranched in the foothills of the Rockies since 1889, said that he had initially liked the idea of separation, but that he had changed his mind. He told the group at the Twin Cities Hotel in Longview, Alberta, that he would vote to remain in Canada because of what it would cost for the province to become an independent nation.

“We can’t pay that money,” said Mr. Cannon, who wore a black cowboy hat. “It doesn’t matter how good we’re doing, that money is huge.”

Hugo Gertin, seated next to Mr. Cannon, dismissed the idea of secession as “crazy talk.” If Alberta leaves Canada, he predicted, “Trump’s going to come through there” and just take control.”

When Rick Quarrel stopped by the table, though, he said it was past time to cut ties with Canada.

“I have got more blood and sweat into the dirt of Alberta than I do anywhere else and I will probably die here — and I hope this vote goes through,” he said. “Alberta’s tired, we’re tired of fighting. This is our way of saying, ‘We are done.’”

Whatever their differing views about separation, the group was united in their disappointment with the province’s premier, Danielle Smith, who called the referendum.

Ms. Smith became the leader of the United Conservative Party largely through the support of separatist activists who had dislodged her predecessor. After a court struck down a petition from separatists to hold a direct vote on quitting Canada, Ms. Smith added the secession question to an already-scheduled referendum on other issues.

She has since said that she will vote to remain in Canada, though she will not require elected members of her party to do the same. That approach has alienated people on both sides of the debate.

Mitch Sylvestre, the head of one of the most prominent separatist groups, characterized Ms. Smith’s position as a betrayal of her party’s base.

“She’s playing a very interesting game that I think has very dire consequences for her,” Mr. Sylvestre, who leads the Alberta Prosperity Project, said in an interview. “I just don’t understand why she’s got to put her thumb on the scale.”

Ms. Smith was conspicuously absent on Thursday and Friday from large pro-Canada rallies in Calgary, Alberta’s largest city, and Edmonton, its capital. At both, Prime Minister Mark Carney was the feature attraction.

After the Calgary event, Thomas Lukaszuk, a former provincial lawmaker who helped organize the rallies, questioned Ms. Smith’s commitment to remaining in Canada. He noted that she has continued to urge separatist legislators not to leave the United Conservative Party.

“For her” he said, “it is more important that separatists stay in her party so that they can win another election than actually doing the right thing for Canada and saying, ‘If you’re for separatism, there is no room for you in this party. Some things are more important than holding on to power.”

Ms. Smith’s office said that she was not available for an interview.

Since Ms. Smith added the separation question to the referendum in May, no clear version has emerged of what an independent Alberta might look like. Nor has any one separatist group come to dominate the public debate.

Some groups have suggested that they want an independent Alberta to be guided by Christian doctrine. One podcast that promotes separatism, “The Lavigne Show,” has posted signs along highways showing a family walking toward an oversize cross and a Christian church at sunrise with the words: “Independence protects our future, our families and our faith.”

Immigration policy, which is addressed by other questions on the referendum ballot, is a major issue for many separatists, including some of those who favor cutting ties with Canada during the discussion at the Twin Cities hotel last week.

“Our immigration here in Alberta is terrible,” Mr. Quarrel told the table, saying that immigrants were “taking over.”

Separatists don’t always agree about what an independent Alberta’s relationship with the United States should look like. Some traveled to Washington last year for meetings, apparently with low-ranking officials at the State Department.

The Globe and Mail recently reported that, at one of those meetings, some secession backers broached several possible deals. Under one of them, if the United States let the oil-rich new nation build a pipeline to the Pacific through Washington State, Alberta would pay royalties and offer a slice of its territory for a railway to Alaska.

Alberta and its neighbor Saskatchewan were created by Canada’s federal government in 1905 on land it had purchased from the Hudson’s Bay Company. But Albertans soon came to resent the federal government.

The tensions grew only worse after a major oil find in 1947, followed by the development of the oil sands in the 1970s, brought the province wealth. Many Albertans were particularly unhappy about the federal government distributing tax dollars to poorer provinces to ensure even standards of services in areas like health care across the country.

After months of campaigning, it appears that the separatists have not won many voters to their cause. A Janet Brown Opinion Research poll for CBC News found that 72 percent of respondents planned to vote to remain in Canada, while 23 percent back a second vote on succession.

Some believe that Ms. Smith may end up paying a price for political opportunism

Craig Snodgrass, the mayor of High River, a town south of Calgary, said Albertans have been politically volatile since the Covid pandemic. Alberta has been home to some of Canada’s largest protests against vaccinations and public health restrictions.

“Covid empowered a lot of people to to fight government, and they’re really comfortable doing it,” he said from his office in Town Hall. “This is just their next thing: We can’t be a part of this country anymore.”

Mr. Snodgrass said that Ms. Smith, whom he views as a close friend, had channeled that pandemic anger through her radio talk show into a political comeback. She once led a right-wing party that formed the United Conservatives through a merger.

Now, he said, her ties to the separatists may come back to bite her.

item.title: ‘The Mystery Continues’: Latest Hunt for Amelia Earhart’s Plane Comes Up Empty
item.description:
Search after search has failed to find the plane of Amelia Earhart, the pioneering pilot who disappeared over the Pacific Ocean in 1937. One recent expedition mistook rocks for the aircraft. Now, another has found trees.

An American team searching a remote atoll in the South Pacific said in a statement on Monday that it had found “no conclusive evidence” of wreckage from Ms. Earhart’s Lockheed 10-E Electra.

What had looked like a metallic Y-shaped fragment in a satellite image was most likely a collection of trees covered with coral sand, the team said.

“This mystery has been ongoing for 90 years, and the mystery continues,” Rick Pettigrew, a member of the expedition, said in a video from an atoll in Kiribati, the Pacific island nation where the search took place.

Here’s what to know Ms. Earhart’s disappearance, the decades-long effort to find her plane and the latest search.

Ms. Earhart was born July 24, 1897, in Atchison, Kan., according to the Federal Aviation Administration. Her father was a lawyer and her grandfather was a judge. After attending school in Chicago, she moved to Toronto in 1918 to become a nurse’s aide in a military hospital.

She took her first plane ride in 1920, an experience that inspired her to become a pilot. “As soon as I left the ground, I knew I myself had to fly,” she declared, according to the National Air and Space Museum at the Smithsonian in Washington.

She began taking flying lessons from Anita Snook, a pioneer of aviation, in 1921 and received an international pilot’s license in 1923.

Ms. Earhart achieved many aviation milestones. She was the first woman to fly to an altitude of 14,000 feet (1922), to fly across the Atlantic Ocean as a passenger (1928) and to make the crossing solo (1932), according to the National Air and Space Museum.

In 1937, she was attempting to become the first woman to fly around the world at the Equator when she and her navigator, Fred Noonan, disappeared over the Pacific Ocean. They had left Papua New Guinea on what was to be the third-to-last leg of the journey and were heading to Howland Island, about 400 miles northwest of Nikumaroro, the remote atoll where the latest search unfolded.

She was 39 when she disappeared and was declared dead in 1939.

After Ms. Earhart and Mr. Noonan disappeared, the U.S. launched one of the largest air-sea searches in history at the time, spending two weeks scouring an area of the Pacific Ocean roughly the size of Texas. That search cost more than $4 million.

Over the following decades, others invested millions in efforts to locate the wreckage of their plane.

Since 1989, a nonprofit organization called the International Group for Historic Aircraft Recovery, or TIGHAR, has led repeated expeditions to Nikumaroro, pursuing a theory that Ms. Earhart and Mr. Noonan landed on the island and eventually died there as castaways.

In 2012, the group led a $2.2 million search that received public support from then-Secretary of State Hillary Clinton. The expedition failed to locate the aircraft, and a sonar image of an underwater object also failed to produce a confirmed discovery.

In 2019, Robert Ballard, the explorer famous for discovering the Titanic, led a two-week, multimillion dollar search. His team came up empty.

In 2024, Tony Romeo, the chief executive of Deep Sea Vision, said a sonar image that his company captured on an $11 million expedition appeared to show a plane resting about three miles below the surface of the Pacific Ocean. The object lay somewhere within a 100-mile radius of Howland Island.

The company later announced on social media that what it had thought was wreckage from the plane was a rock formation.

The disappearance has recently drawn renewed attention from Washington. Last year, President Trump called on the federal government to unseal all remaining classified files on Ms. Earhart, a trove of more than 4,600 pages of documents.

The Taraia Object expedition, a joint effort by the Archaeological Legacy Institute, Purdue Research Foundation and Purdue University, was looking for an object with a reflective surface that it first saw in a satellite image of the Nikumaroro atoll in 2020. The team thought the object could be a metallic fragment from Ms. Earhart’s plane, which had been originally purchased with money from the Purdue Research Foundation.

TIGHAR’s longtime leader, Ric Gillespie, was skeptical, arguing before the team arrived that the object was probably a fallen tree.

By the time the team of 17 arrived at the island last week, a large portion of the material they had once seen in the satellite imagery had washed away, leaving a smaller, Y-shaped fragment. In its statement on Monday, the team said the fragment was most likely part of a collection of trees coated in a shiny, hardened mixture of coral sand.

Despite the findings, the expedition said its members continue to support TIGHAR’s theory that Ms. Earhart and Mr. Noonan survived as castaways on the atoll.

item.title: Priest Dies After Crucifix Falls on Him During Livestreamed Mass
item.description:
A priest in Ecuador died on Saturday after a large wooden crucifix fell from a wall and fatally struck him during a livestreamed Mass.

The Rev. Patricio Alfredo Sánchez Molinari, the pastor of Our Lady of Perpetual Help Church in the city of Guayaquil, was speaking to his congregation on Saturday when the accident occurred.

In a video streamed live to the priest’s Facebook page and verified by The New York Times, Father Sánchez Molinari stood in a flower-filled sanctuary framed by a sweeping wall mural dominated by a large crucifix. He put on his reading glasses and began speaking — “Let us pray to the Lord” — moments before the crucifix detached from the wall. Facing his congregation, the priest did not see the cross falling behind him, and he collapsed upon impact.

Parishioners in the nave could be heard shouting in shock and several rushed to the altar to help before the video cut out. It was unclear what caused the crucifix to fall. Local authorities did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The Archdiocese of Guayaquil confirmed the priest’s death in a statement on social media on Sunday, writing that he had “departed for the Father’s House to rejoice in His presence and glory.”

Mourners gathered at the church on Sunday evening for a service in the priest’s honor.

item.title: A Tycoon Linked to Haitian Gangs Has Died
item.description:
Gilbert Bigio, a Haitian industrialist widely described as the country’s first billionaire, and who was sanctioned by Canada for ties to criminal gangsin his homeland, died on Sept. 29 in Florida. He was 91.

His death was reported in the Haitian press.

With interests in steel, energy, logistics, consumer goods, construction and banking, Mr. Bigio’s holding company, long known as the GB Group and eventually renamed BGO, touched the impoverished island nation’s economy in every corner.

Mr. Bigio’s family remain major players in what the International Monetary Fund and others have described as Haiti’s tiny economic elite. BGO supplies cooking oils and soap to Haitian households, steel from Haiti’s only steel mill to its builders and deepwater port facilities to its shippers. BGO became a regional economic force as well, owning gas stations in Jamaica and the Dominican Republic.

The elite plays an outsize role in Haiti’s chaotic politics, and Mr. Bigio appears not to have been an exception, though he stayed largely out of public view and rarely granted interviews. In December 2022, Canada sanctioned him, along with two other Haitian businessmen.

“Canada has reason to believe these individuals are using their status as high-profile members of the economic elite in Haiti to protect and enable the illegal activities of armed criminal gangs, including through money laundering and other acts of corruption,” a foreign ministry statement said.

“The sanctions Canada has imposed are intended to put pressure on those responsible for the ongoing violence and instability in Haiti,” the statement continued. “These people must stop providing funds and weapons to criminal gangs in Haiti.”

According to Reuters, the GB Group did not immediately reply to the sanctions; one Haiti expert, Jake Johnston, of the Center for Economic Policy and Research in Washington, said in an interview that Canada’s decision was a largely “symbolic” move with little practical impact. Members of Mr. Bigio’s family did not respond in recent days to queries for this obituary.

How The Times decides who gets an obituary. There is no formula, scoring system or checklist in determining the news value of a life. We investigate, research and ask around before settling on our subjects. If you know of someone who might be a candidate for a Times obituary, please suggest it here.

Mr. Johnston said Mr. Bigio’s immense wealth — he bought an ultraluxury $132,000 Mercedes Maybach from the estate of the disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein, The Miami Herald reported — was important to contrast with the brutal poverty of his native land.

“You can’t separate them from the broader context,” he said. “These are the elites who have benefited for decades from a status quo that very obviously does not work for a majority of Haitians.”

In a text message, Fritz Alphonse Jean, the former director of Haiti’s central bank and a former prime minister, noting the steady growth of Mr. Bigio’s company, wrote that “the capital that enabled this expansion was largely generated from Haiti’s economy, itself shaped by weak institutions that were incapable of ensuring a level playing field for all businesses.”

Mr. Jean criticized the absence of “meaningful integration of social responsibility into the operations of the country’s wealthiest enterprises.”

The I.M.F., in its 2025 report, noted that “many if not all gangs regularly cooperate with elites to serve oligarchic interests through kidnapping, murder, and the intimidation of neighborhoods.”

In the absence of a functional government, especially after the assassination in 2021 of President Jovenel Moïse, the gangs now have a virtual stranglehold on political and economic life in the country. They are said to control 70 percent of the capital, Port-au-Prince, and the country’s major highways.

For Mr. Johnston, it is almost inevitable that the country’s leading businessman had some kind of relationship with the gangs.

“If you’re running a port in Port-au-Prince, you’re engaging with armed actors. It’s a condition of doing business,” he said. “The cargo doesn’t leave that port without payments.” He noted that “the story of that port and its relationship with arms trafficking is well established.”

Canada’s sanctions were at least the second time Mr. Bigio had been subject to government strictures. The U.S. Treasury Department reportedly froze assets held in U.S. banks by Mr. Bigio and other prominent Haitians whom the department alleged backed the 1991 military coup that ousted Jean-Bertrand Aristide, Haiti’s first democratically elected president. Sanctions against Mr. Bigio and members of his family were removed after Mr. Aristide’s return in 1994 following U.S. intervention.

Mr. Bigio, the scion of immigrant Sephardic Jews from Syria who was Israel’s honorary consul in Haiti for 25 years, spent some of his time in a 9,200 -square-foot mansion on a man-made island in Biscayne Bay called Indian Creek. Accessible by only a guarded bridge, it is known in Miami as the “Billionaire Bunker”; the Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, among others, have property there.

The Haitian businessman was extensively named in the 2021 Pandora Papers leak, a trove of financial records naming dozens of wealthy individuals who had set up shell companies in tax havens.

“Bigio was connected to at least a dozen such companies, many of which were created in the Bahamas,” the Washington-based International Consortium of Investigative Journalists, which helped disseminate the Pandora Papers, wrote in an online report.

The real-world consequences of this financial sleight-of-hand were dire in Haiti, the poorest country in the Western Hemisphere, the I.M.F. noted in 2020. Between 2015 and that year, Haiti collected tax revenues equivalent to about 13 percent of its economy, ranking it above only Panama and Venezuela.

When Mr. Bigio gave an interview, in 2004 with The Herald, it was to deny any political role in his country. He preferred to talk about his part in supporting Jewish ritual, hosting gatherings on High Holy Days, in a country with only a handful of Jews. For years, a large Israeli flag flew in front of his mansion in Pétion-Ville, an affluent neighborhood in the capital. He kept Haiti’s only Torah in his study.

“Our principle, which we respect daily, is not to mix in Haitian politics,” he told The Herald. But that statement ran counter to the observations of the I.M.F., which wrote in its 2025 analysis that “the community of economic elites in Haiti is relatively small but it holds significant influence over politicians,” and that, “like politicians, some of economic elites employ gangs for close protection.”

Gilbert Bigio was born in Port-au-Prince on June 10, 1935, into a family that had come to Haiti from Syria at the end of the 19th century and made its fortune in the cotton-, cacao- and wood-export businesses.

With other investors, he founded Aciérie d’Haiti, the country’s first steel mill, in 1972, and it became the basis for the diversified GB Group. The group employed more than 2,000 people “at the height of his influence,” according to an obituary published by Memorial Keepers. GB Group was the principal developer of Port Lafito, Haiti’s first deepwater container terminal, which opened in 2015.

Mr. Bigio stepped down as head of the conglomerate in 2018 in favor of his son, Reuven. In addition to his son, survivors include his wife, Monique; and two daughters, Yael and Laurence.

Mr. Bigio “built industries where none existed, employed thousands, and gave generously, while also accumulating power in ways that drew international scrutiny,” according to the obituary in Memorial Keepers.

Mr. Johnston, the analyst, dismissed the argument frequently invoked by Haiti’s elites that “‘without us, you would all starve,’” noting that “they have a stranglehold on the economy. Have you been upholding transparency? Have you been paying taxes?”

André Paultre contributed reporting from Port-au-Prince. Sheelagh McNeill and Susan C. Beachy contributed research.

item.title: Houthi Strikes Kill Dozens in Yemeni Desert Military Camp, Officials Say
item.description:
The Iranian-backed Houthi militia killed dozens of Yemeni soldiers in a strike on a desert camp in the middle of the country on Monday, officials said, in what appeared to be one of the deadliest attacks since their war resumed.

Col. Majed al-Nuzaili, a spokesman for the Yemeni armed forces, said in a statement on social media that the Houthis had fired three ballistic missiles at the Al Alam camp in Shabwa Province, hitting what he described as a training center for security and police recruits. He told the Saudi-owned broadcaster Al Arabiya that at least 47 had been killed and 53 others wounded.

Saba, a Houthi-run news agency, said the group had struck what it called Saudi “troop buildups” at the camp and made no mention of recruits. The Yemeni government and the Houthis, a rebel group from the country’s north, have been at war since 2014, when the militia seized the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, which it still holds.

“The number of martyrs is very high and is expected to rise,” Fahd Al-Khulaifi, the deputy governor of Shabwa Province, said in a telephone interview. He said there were dozens of casualties, some of whom were being transferred to the government-held cities of Aden and Al Mukalla. The Saudi-led military coalition that is fighting the Houthis in Yemen has not commented on the strike.

Graphic footage published on social media and verified by The New York Times showed multiple bodies and blood on paved ground in Al Alam camp. At least 15 bodies can be seen as the camera pans, with clothes and sandals strewed around.

The scale of the attack underscored the rapidly intensifying war in Yemen, which erupted earlier this year after the United States and Israel attacked Iran, the Houthis’ main patron.

In recent weeks, forces affiliated with the Yemeni government have attempted to retake strategic territory on the country’s Red Sea coast that the Houthis seized in a lightning offensive last month.

As the fighting has ground on, the Houthis have demonstrated their ability to hold out against the government’s forces, which Saudi warplanes have supported, and the militia has launched offensive strikes deep within government-held regions. On Friday, the Houthis struck the Yemeni government’s headquarters in Aden, killing five staff and security officers.

The conflict has also increasingly spilled onto Saudi soil, as the Houthis have attacked infrastructure and oil facilities in the kingdom. Frequent attacks on an airport in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, have killed at least 17 people and injured more than 330 others since the beginning of this month, according to the Saudi authorities.

Saudi Arabia further restricted flights to and from its main airport in Riyadh this weekend, saying that no flights would be allowed to arrive or depart without explicit permission. The change was made in an official notice that took effect on Saturday night local time, with no end date.

Rashad al-Alimi, who leads Yemen’s internationally recognized government, the Presidential Leadership Council, promised a “decisive response” to the attack on Monday, saying the deaths would not stop the government from protecting citizens and rebuilding state institutions. His comments were reported by the Saba news agency.

The Houthis’ long conflict with the Yemeni government and its allies previously came to a cease-fire in 2022 but tensions resurfaced this year over the summer after the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of carrying out an airstrike on Sanaa’s airport and retaliated by imposing a blockade on Saudi maritime traffic.

Shuaib Almosawa contributed reporting from Sanaa, Yemen, Niraj Chokshi from New York, and Sanjana Varghese from London.

item.title: Two Die at Raucous Religious Festival in Japan. Will Anything Change?
item.description:
Every autumn, hundreds of Japanese people come together and dash down streets while pulling ornate wooden floats in the shape of shrines, a tradition known as danjiri.

But recent deaths and accidents are feeding anxiety about the ritual and bringing a somber note to the end of the mid-autumn festival season.

Osaka’s police department reported two deaths and several injuries in danjiri festivals in the cities of Izumiotsu and Izumisano on Oct. 10. In both instances, the floats, which weigh several tons, toppled over while turning corners, crushing participants who were standing on the side.

Because danjiri performances are rooted in religious tradition, a board of community leaders, rather than the police, decides the rules and safety protocols. The local police are investigating the circumstances of the deaths, but most organizers have stopped short of abolishing the sharp turns or calling for them to be taken more slowly.

“Heatstroke, falls and bone fractures are common occurrences here every year — though, ideally, no one should get hurt,” said Katsunori Fujita, 71, a chairman of the liaison council in Izumiotsu, who helps decide on the rules for the parades in his district.

Mr. Fujita witnessed the accident in Izumiotsu as he patrolled as a volunteer. He said he would continue enforcing safety precautions and instruct participants on where to escape during trial runs. But his district was unlikely to change the rules and the police were unlikely to intervene in the Shinto religious rite, he said.

The danjiri tradition dates back three centuries and began as a religious ritual during harvest season. Residents of Kishiwada, the southern city in Osaka prefecture where the tradition began, would carry a wooden float lit by hundreds of paper lanterns around the town before communal prayers at a Shinto shrine.

Over time, danjiri spread to other cities across Japan. It also became more violent. Scuffles often broke out as floats jostled each other on narrow streets. The frequent tussles led to danjiri becoming known as the “fighting festival."

In the 1950s, community leaders in Kishiwada began to establish new rules to address the violence, including introducing a one-way system to avoid collisions between floats. It has since evolved into a parade with great displays of showmanship. Performers in traditional uniforms balance and dance on the roofs of the floats, which themselves are symbols of the vitality of each local community. Children are recruited to take part while in elementary school, practicing the sharp turns with hand-pulled wagons.

During the parade, young and old residents run ahead of each float, pulling it with ropes. They execute sharp 90-degree turns, known as yarimawashi, at full speed, as performers riding on the float lean in one direction to prevent it from tipping over.

But safety questions have been raised year after year. The fatalities earlier this month were not the first.

In 2022 and 2023, four people died and 32 were injured in four incidences. One danjiri participant died in Maniwa, a city in Okayama, leading to a one-year hiatus of the festival before it resumed in 2025. In 2023, police in Tondabayashi, a city in Osaka, accused three danjiri festival representatives of negligence after one death and three injuries, but prosecutors did not indict them.

Other festivals involving heavy floats have suffered fatalities. On Saturday, the deputy mayor of Saijo on Shikoku Island was killed while raising on his shoulders a three-ton float called a taikodai, which serves as a moving stage for drummers.

Hisao Arimoto, an associate professor who studies the danjiri festival at Konan Women’s University in Kobe, said that there had been calls for bans or changes every year, but few changes had followed. “It would be difficult to make drastic changes because it is an event that involves so many people,” he said by telephone.

Hideaki Karaki, a professor emeritus of the University of Tokyo, said that it would be impossible to eliminate risks altogether. “The very elements that create danger — its speed, its weight and the intense energy of the crowd — are also the core of what makes the festival so compelling,” he wrote in Wedge Online, a news and business magazine.

But he added that the accidents would continue if organizers claim that they had taken enough precautions without conducting proper risk assessments. “To ensure that a 300-year-old tradition can endure for another 300 years, what is required is the courage to look the dangers squarely in the eye,” he wrote.

item.title: Our Interview With María Corina Machado
item.description:
María Corina Machado is Venezuela’s most popular opposition leader. But she has not been able to return to her country since last year, when she left to receive the Nobel Peace Prize. Since then, the Trump administration captured Venezuela’s autocratic leader, Nicolás Maduro, on Jan. 3, 2026, and installed his vice president, Delcy Rodríguez, passing over Ms. Machado for the leadership spot.

Ms. Machado’s political movement won Venezuela’s 2024 presidential vote, even as the state arrested, beat and imprisoned her supporters. But the ruling party refused to give up power, and it continues to govern under President Trump.

Ms. Machado wants to return to Venezuela and run for president in another election. She spoke this week with Julie Turkewitz, the Andes bureau chief for The New York Times. They met in Panama, where Ms. Machado is staying.

Here are excerpts from the wide-ranging interview, in which Ms. Machado criticized the Trump administration’s handpicked partner in Venezuela and spoke about her country’s future.

I want to start by talking about where we are now. Have you been sidelined politically by the United States?

This is a really transformational moment. I believe that Venezuela has had a cultural change for the good, even though it went through this ordeal of 27 years, and so much devastation.

What we have done in these last years is something that is unstoppable and irreversible.

So probably we have different time frames with the United States government, but I have no doubt that we have the same vision in terms of a democratic transition. And in that sense, you cannot sideline the will of a people that have decided to be free and that have organized themselves to achieve it.

Do you agree with the decision by the U.S. to keep Delcy Rodríguez in power?

That was a possibility. She’s certainly doing whatever she’s been told. And that can be comfortable for certain interests in terms of moving smoothly.

I believe it could have been done, certainly, without her because she’s part of the criminal system. But it is what it is, and here’s where we are, and as I said before, it’s in the interest of the Venezuelan people that this works.

If you become the next leader of the country, what is your specific plan for what happens to the high-level leaders of the current government? You have talked about the idea of justice. Specifically what does that process look like?

We want Venezuela to change, so something that we certainly will not do is act as the regime has done, violating human rights and violating the Constitution. So certainly, we’re determined to offer justice and respect for the rights of even those people that violated our own rights.

Because this has to be the foundation of an institutional framework that will last for generations to come. So we’re not moved by revenge or hate.

We are moved by the truth and the fact that we have to assure that those crimes will never be repeated in Venezuela.

Our proposal is to create a truth commission that’s integrated by individuals that have respect and credibility in all of Venezuelan society and can address, case by case, how to move forward, taking into account not only the severity, the seriousness of the crimes committed, but also the disposition of every individual to ask for forgiveness, to facilitate the process, to facilitate justice.

Would some of the highest figures — for example Delcy Rodriguez, Interior Minister Diosdado Cabello — face possible prison charges in a new government?

[As vice president under Mr. Maduro, Ms. Rodríguez helped lead a government in which human rights abuses were common. The Trump administration imposed sanctions on her in 2018, calling her a key figure in solidifying Mr. Maduro’s authoritarian rule; it lifted the sanctions this year after choosing her as Venezuela’s leader.

As interior minister in charge of the police and prisons, Mr. Cabello has overseen widespread repression in Venezuela, the U.N. says. The Trump administration imposed sanctions on him as well, and named him as a defendant in a Jan. 3 drug trafficking indictment against Maduro, but he remains in Ms. Rodríguez’s government.]

In our Constitution and international treaties, there are crimes that are not subject to amnesty or forgiveness. You know, human rights violations and crimes against humanity or terrorism.

I believe it should be an independent commission that addresses this issue, and I believe no one should beforehand state what is going to be the punishment for those who have committed crimes.

But prison would be on the table?

In a country so hurt by systematic, massive crime, the notion of impunity could be very, very dangerous because that could turn sectors of the population against the process, because people demand justice, and that’s absolutely legitimate.

What happens to lower-ranking individuals, like the guard in El Rodeo prison, who maybe engaged in torture but says they were responding to an order from above? Does that person face justice? Does that person go to prison?

You’re mentioning just one case, but this extends to practically every sector. So yes, Venezuelan society will have to make compromises so that we can move forward.

And that’s why the truth commission is so important, because we are not ignoring it. We are addressing it. Things should be known first of all, and recognition to the victims and reparations to the victims is absolutely a priority.

Do you think that the U.S. would have to enforce the results of an election? And how would it do that?

No, I don’t think so. Not today. It should have been done two years ago.

What should have happened specifically two years ago?

Well, the Venezuelan people organized, voted and proved a landslide victory on July 28, 2024. I believe the international community as a whole should have enforced that result.

Are you angry at the Biden administration for not doing more after July 2024?

I think the international community as a whole never decided to act decisively. And I think it was a horrible precedent because the message you send to societies is that at the end they are on their own.

Would you have welcomed military action by the U.S.?

Such as what happened Jan. 3, yes.

Why has the U.S. not facilitated your return to Venezuela?

There is no one other person in Venezuela that wants this three-stage process to succeed. [The United States has said its involvement in Venezuela will have three phases: stabilization, economic recovery and transition to democracy.]

I believe that my presence in Venezuela is a significant factor to help and to strengthen the success of the process.

So the fact that I go back will help channel all this growing anxiety that we’re seeing in so many demonstrations and protests.

I would say that whoever opposes my presence in Venezuela does not want the process to be successful.

Are there people in the Trump administration who also do not want you to return?

I think there are, in the United States, in different sectors, people that truly support my return, and people that have doubts that it could be done in a safe way.

The U.S. has enormous power in Venezuela. Why has Marco Rubio, for example, not facilitated your return?

I don’t know the answer in terms of his decision, but I can tell you what he has told me. And he has been very clear in terms of my right to go back to my country — and that the president had told Delcy Rodríguez that I should not be harmed when I go back. And I believe in his word.

I know you have a relationship that goes back years with Marco Rubio. What is you relationship like now? How often do you communicate?

I will keep that private because I’ve learned that in order to build long-lasting relationships you have to act with prudence.

What happened when you tried to go back to Venezuela after the June earthquakes?

Well, the first time I tried to go through Curaçao, and my plane was ordered to turn around, I was on the plane in the air. And the second time I came to Panama, I bought tickets on a commercial flight and the regime closed the air zone in Venezuela.

I just want to confirm, were there seven attempts in total to return?

Yes.

You don’t know or won’t say who was it specifically that stopped you?

I don’t know, and I prefer not to speculate, but I certainly believe that the government of Venezuela, the regime in Venezuela, was involved.

Are you concerned that coming back to Venezuela you will encounter lack of energy, fear, people becoming comfortable-ish with the situation? Are you concerned that people might not go into the streets?

Look what is happening already, and I’m not there. One the one hand, you are seeing the expressions of former political prisoners, union leaders, teachers.

They are already expressing themselves for the first time in many, many years in this way. And that’s one of the positive results of Jan. 3.

We want to turn this into a massive discussion in small assemblies, tiny assemblies, thousands of them all around the country and using technology and A.I. — we already have a platform — in order to gather all that and truly listen to what Venezuelan people are saying.

Would you keep the Chevron deal as is?

I wouldn’t be surprised if representatives of this company and others that have signed contracts right now would like to improve the terms of their contracts once we’re done.

The fact that we will have a transparent and attractive fiscal system that can be stable for the long term, and the fact we will offer international arbitration, all of this impacts directly on your rate of return and make all these investments much more profitable.

How do you get the government of Delcy Rodríguez to hand over power?

Delcy Rodríguez today follows instructions that come from the U.S. government. President Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio have stated a three-phase plan that includes a transition.

There are options, but certainly the fact that the U.S. has currently top members of the regime facing justice in the United States makes very clear what’s the alternative.

But a very real dilemma that you face is that by all signs Delcy Rodríguez is doing whatever the U.S. asks. The Trump administration really has enormous control to do whatever it wants in Venezuela. In a new government under María Corina Machado, the Trump administration might not be able to have so much control. Why should the Trump administration want to give up its current situation?

I do not see a dilemma there, because if you have to choose between fear and conviction in terms of your ally, your partner, you would certainly go for the second.

This Trump administration is very focused on striking deals and getting benefits as opposed to larger ideals or convictions of democracy.

I think that from every perspective you address the Venezuelan situation right now, it is a win-win situation to move ahead into the transition.

From the migration perspective, you have over a million Venezuelans in the U.S. Sixty-five percent of them say they want to go back if there is a democratic transition.

And you need to have a partner that truly is committed to dismantling the terror regime, not to try to accommodate until a later moment in which they could bring it back to the previous state.

And third, from an economic and energy perspective, yes, some deals are being made now, but it’s a fraction of what will be made once we have security, stability and legitimacy in Venezuela.

And I think the greatest legacy President Trump will have in this hemisphere is being able to have a nation that rebuilds its institutions and that turns into the strongest ally of the U.S. in the region.

When you saw President Trump come out on Jan. 3 and say, “María Corina doesn’t have the support inside the country” — after you did all of the things that we know that you did in your country — what was your response in that moment?

My assessment was that he was referring to the security forces. And I believe that certainly in the top brass, there are individuals that have persecuted me and our team for years — for years. And in that very small group certainly I do not have support.

But they [Trump officials] know better than anybody what the rest of the armed forces and the police forces in Venezuela feel and believe. Their support for our movement is huge.

Were you angry in that moment?

I was surprised.

Do you need the U.S. on your side for there to be a free and fair election?

Certainly we do. And I trust we will — we do have them. We do have the U.S. government. And I believe we have the U.S. Congress, in both parties.

But even further, I believe the American people support our cause.

This is going to work, this is going to prove to the world that even the most cruel, corrupt tyranny can be dismantled because of the will of a people and the support of democratic leaders.

And this is why this movement is so powerful, because it’s driven by values and virtues and it has to do with the truth, it has do with transparency. And it has to do with good.

And I should ask, to have it on the record, When are you going back to Venezuela?

Sooner than you would expect.

After the interview, Ms. Machado clarified some details in a phone call, and Ms. Turkewitz asked about negotiations happening between Venezuelan officials and a different faction of the opposition, which have the goal of setting an election framework.

Did you choose not to participate in these talks, or did the U.S. not invite you?

I think it is clear to everyone by now that the United States government was the one that decided how to assemble this team from both sides. And I have been very clear. I am not part of the commission; I am also not going to stand in the way. Rather — for the sake of Venezuela and for our own well-being — we all hope that what was promised is fulfilled.
